new_statements.translation: [when the determined segments] ... bear the accent on the penultimate, the bound forms are full. ... [when they] bear the accent on the antepenultimate, that is, ordinarily, when these segments contain the terminals -tsy or -ky, the bound forms are full, except in the first and second persons singular where they may appear [reduced] ... the terminals -tsy and -ky are kept or dropped at the speaker's discretion.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bara follows the general Malagasy pattern: word accent on the penultimate syllable by default; words ending in the weak terminals -tsy / -ky (Bara reflexes of Merina -tra / -ka; Merina -na is lost in Bara) are ordinarily accented on the antepenultimate; suffixation shifts the radical's accent one syllable rightward; in article+noun and compound groups the main accent is on the last (determined) element, earlier elements keeping at most a secondary accent. Faublee 1947:7 confirms accent placement is rule-governed ('regles fixes') and that the accented vowel is also long; Howe 2017:48 states the same penult/weak-final-antepenult system pan-Malagasy with '-ke, -tse in western and southwestern dialects (Dahl 1952)'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rabenilaina (snippet): proclitic articles (ny, ley, lei) bear only 'un accent secondaire', main accent on the determined element; Howe 2017:48-49 (pan-Malagasy): secondary stress on certain syllables before the primary in long words and on original tonic syllables of non-final compound members.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenult accent tied to weak terminals -tsy/-ky, which speakers may drop (yielding surface variation); Howe 2017: 'a small number of words have final-syllable stress'; en.wikipedia (unsourced) notes Bara loss of final -na giving contrastive pairs like tana 'hand' (penult) vs tana 'village' (final, < tanana).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent of radicals and suffixed forms; Rabenilaina's snippets concern accent of the host noun/verb conditioning enclitic genitive pronoun allomorphy and accent in determiner+noun groups; Faublee marks accent in running Bara texts only where distinctive.
new_statements.identity_note: Rabenilaina 1974/1983 describe the Bara ('bàra') dialect of the Ihosy-Betroka region (his native variety); Faublee 1947's texts are Bara of the Ihosy/Horombe area. Howe 2017 and Adelaar (2013, as summarised by Howe pp. 23-24) split 'Eastern Bara' (Central group) from 'Western Bara' (Western group), so a single stress statement is assumed to cover both; all fall under Glottolog bara1369 [bhr]. Do not confuse with Tucanoan Bara/Waimaha (fr.wikipedia 'Bara (langue)', Glottolog waim1255) or Bodo-Garo 'Bara' cited in Les langues du monde.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3.6 p. 48: 'Most words have primary lexical stress on the penultimate syllable. However, lexical items ending in one of the weak final syllables (-na, -ka, -tra in Merina; -ke, -tse in western and southwestern dialects (Dahl 1952)..) have antepenultimate stress, and a small number of words have final-syllable stress'; suffixation shifts stress one syllable right; secondary stress on earlier syllables in long words; compounds keep primary stress on rightmost member. Pan-Malagasy; Bara speakers (Ihosy) used in production study but no Bara-specific stress sentence.

sources.note: Ch. VI 'L'accent tonique' pp. 236-245: Malagasy radical themes -- disyllables generally paroxytone, trisyllables generally proparoxytone (anaka, tanana) sometimes paroxytone, all monosyllables accented, accented vowel long, suffix moves accent to following vowel, reduplications/compounds keep accent on last member. 'Bara de Ihosy' is dialect no. 30 and Bara forms are cited passim, but no Bara-specific accent statement.
Unsourced 'Characteristics': final -na of trisyllables dropped (tana 'hand' vs tana-with-final-accent 'village' < tanana / tanana); no stress rule stated.
